title: Bank Regulation Affects Monetary Policy Transmission - San Francisco Fed
gist: Using Fed Y-14Q supervisory data, Greenwald, Krainer and Paul show that during 2022–23 banks with larger unhedged AFS securities losses cut business lending, almost entirely at banks that must count AOCI in regulatory capital. A calibrated model implies that marking all securities to market in capital would amplify monetary tightening, lowering bank-dependent firms' investment ~9pp more after a year, linking bank regulation (AOCI rules) directly to monetary policy strength.

insights.claim: During the 2022–23 Fed tightening cycle, large U.S. banks with bigger losses on their securities portfolios extended less credit to firms, per Federal Reserve Y-14Q supervisory data (Greenwald, Krainer, Paul 2026).
insights.speaker: Daniel l Greenwald
insights.so_what: Rate hikes hit corporate credit supply not only via loan pricing but via bank securities losses; watch bank unrealized losses as a leading indicator of C&I lending tightening.
insights.quote: banks with larger losses on securities during the 2022–23 monetary policy tightening cycle extended less credit to firms

insights.claim: The lending cutback from securities losses is driven by unhedged available-for-sale (AFS) securities; value changes on held-to-maturity (HTM) securities and hedged AFS securities produce substantially smaller and statistically insignificant lending effects.
insights.speaker: Daniel l Greenwald
insights.so_what: Banks' AFS share and hedge ratio determine how much a rate shock bleeds into their lending; HTM-heavy or well-hedged banks are less credit-sensitive to rates.

insights.claim: Banks required to include AOCI (unrealized AFS gains/losses) in regulatory capital cut lending several times more in response to securities losses than other banks, and the response of non-AOCI-capital banks cannot be statistically distinguished from zero.
insights.speaker: Daniel l Greenwald
insights.so_what: Regulatory capital, not economic losses per se, is the binding channel — credit effects concentrate at banks whose capital ratios mark securities to market.
insights.quote: We find lending responses are several times stronger for AOCI-capital banks

insights.claim: Changes in regulatory capital are the primary channel through which interest-rate-driven securities value changes transmit into bank-to-firm credit, since a fall in AOCI forces AOCI-capital banks to raise capital or shrink risk-weighted assets, e.g. by cutting loans.
insights.speaker: Daniel l Greenwald
insights.so_what: A rate shock that erodes AOCI at constrained banks implies deleveraging via loan cuts or equity raises — relevant for bank equity issuance and loan growth forecasts.

insights.claim: Agency mortgage-backed securities and Treasuries account for about 85% of large U.S. bank securities portfolios, so their dominant risk is interest rate risk rather than default risk.
insights.speaker: Daniel l Greenwald
insights.so_what: Bank securities books are effectively a large duration trade; rate moves, not credit events, drive their capital swings.

insights.claim: Around 60% of large U.S. bank securities were classified available-for-sale (marked to market) in Q4 2021, with the rest held-to-maturity at book value, and only 19% of AFS assets carried an accounting hedge.
insights.speaker: Daniel l Greenwald
insights.so_what: Most AFS exposure was unhedged going into 2022, maximizing the pass-through of rate hikes to bank equity.

insights.claim: U.S. regulators excluded AOCI from regulatory capital until 2013, ended the exclusion for larger advanced-approaches banks in 2013, then reinstated it in the Fed's 2019 tailoring rule for all but the largest or most systemically important banks.
insights.speaker: Daniel l Greenwald
insights.so_what: Midsize banks currently carry an AOCI opt-out; any rollback of the 2019 tailoring treatment directly changes their capital sensitivity to rates.

insights.claim: Because midsize regional banks' unrealized securities losses did not pass through to regulatory capital, they looked well capitalized ahead of the March 2023 regional bank runs despite large rate-driven losses that are widely believed to have sparked depositor withdrawals.
insights.speaker: Daniel l Greenwald
insights.so_what: Reported regulatory capital ratios can mask duration losses at midsize banks; use AOCI-adjusted capital when assessing regional bank risk.
insights.quote: these banks appeared relatively well capitalized from a regulatory perspective despite their risk exposure

insights.claim: Broadening AOCI inclusion in regulatory capital would force banks with securities losses to rebuild capital ratios (e.g. by raising equity), lowering collapse risk, but would also push them to cut lending to households and businesses to shrink risk-weighted assets.
insights.speaker: Daniel l Greenwald
insights.so_what: AOCI-reform is a trade-off between financial stability and credit availability; reform proposals imply more equity issuance and procyclical lending in hiking cycles.

insights.claim: In a structural model calibrated to the 2022–23 tightening, bank-dependent firms cut investment about 2.5 percentage points more after one year in the current regime (some securities marked to market) than in a hypothetical economy where all securities are held at book value.
insights.speaker: Daniel l Greenwald
insights.so_what: Mark-to-market capital rules already add a meaningful drag on capex of bank-reliant firms during hikes.

insights.claim: If all bank securities were marked to market in regulatory capital, the model shows investment of bank-dependent firms about 9 percentage points lower one year after a 2022–23-sized tightening than under a no-mark-to-market regime, even after banks hold fewer securities.
insights.speaker: Daniel l Greenwald
insights.so_what: Full AOCI inclusion would sharply strengthen rate-hike pass-through to small/bank-reliant firms' capex — the Fed would need smaller hikes for the same effect.

insights.claim: Bank capital regulation and monetary policy are inherently linked: requiring all banks to reflect securities gains and losses in regulatory capital would make monetary policy more potent, with stronger effects on credit supply and investment.
insights.speaker: Daniel l Greenwald
insights.so_what: Changes to AOCI rules should be read as a monetary-policy event too — they alter how much tightening the economy feels per basis point.
insights.quote: while bank regulation and monetary policy are often considered separately, we show that the two are inherently linked
